one_liner: Zig proactor event loop (io_uring, epoll, kqueue, WASI) with a C API; its HttpArena server ties libreactorng and beats h2o, nginx, Drogon.
what_it_does: libxev is a cross-platform event loop for timers, TCP/UDP sockets, files, processes and cross-thread wakeups (Async), written in Zig and exporting a C-compatible API (include/xev.h). It follows a proactor model modelled on io_uring: the caller submits work with a caller-owned Completion and a callback and is told when the operation has completed, not when the fd is ready. It is not a drop-in for libuv, libev or libevent; it has its own high-level, platform-agnostic API plus a low-level per-backend API. The measured artefact is a 362-line HTTP/1.1 server in the HttpArena repository (frameworks/libxev/src/main.zig) built on libxev, not code shipped by libxev.
how_it_is_fast: On Linux the default backend is io_uring: accept, read and write are submitted as ring operations and completed in batches, so a request costs no readiness syscall round-trip; completions are caller-allocated and the README promises zero runtime allocations inside the loop. Zig's lazy compilation tree-shakes unused watchers out of the binary. The HttpArena server adds the usual throughput recipe on top: one forked worker per CPU in the affinity mask, each with its own 4096-entry ring and SO_REUSEPORT listener, TCP_NODELAY, picohttpparser (C, -O3) for parsing, and a hand-written response with only Content-Type, Content-Length and Connection headers. The io_uring ring is created with flags 0: no SQPOLL, multishot accept/recv or provided/registered buffers (issue #58 open since 2023).
when_to_use: Zig programs (or C programs willing to link a Zig-built library) that want one completion-based event loop across Linux io_uring, epoll fallback, macOS kqueue and WASI.

Linux network servers with many keep-alive connections where an io_uring loop per core with SO_REUSEPORT is the intended architecture; in HttpArena that design matched the best C io_uring entry (libreactorng) and used slightly less CPU per request at fixed rates.
Embedded or latency-sensitive code that needs predictable memory: completions are caller-owned and the loop does not allocate at runtime.
Terminal or desktop apps already in the Zig ecosystem (Ghostty and zml use it) that need timers, process watching and file IO on one loop.
when_not_to_use: You want a measured speedup over a good C io_uring loop: against libreactorng the HttpArena numbers are a tie (+0.1% baseline, -0.5% limited-conn), and the libxev README itself declines to publish benchmarks.

Windows production use: an IOCP backend exists (src/backend/iocp.zig) but the README still lists the Windows backend as planned, and issues #227 (completion reuse corrupts the IOCP loop) and #81 (thread panic) are open.
You need an HTTP server, TLS, HTTP/2 or routing: libxev provides none of them; the HttpArena entry is a minimal handler using picohttpparser and answers every path with the /baseline11 sum.
Toolchain stability matters: it requires Zig 0.16 exactly (stable releases only, no nightlies), does not integrate with Zig 0.16 std.Io, and the README warns integrating it will break the API.
Heavy use of cancel or completion reuse across queues: open issues #233 (io_uring cancel matches reused user_data), #231 (epoll leaks the duplicated fd of cancelled TCP ops), #234 and #169.

integration.form: module (Zig package via build.zig.zon) or static/shared C library built with zig build install
integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond OS APIs; the C library links libc; building needs Zig 0.16
integration.min_toolchain: Zig 0.16.0 (minimum_zig_version in build.zig.zon; libxev tracks stable Zig releases only)
integration.platforms: Linux (io_uring, epoll), macOS (kqueue), WASI (poll_oneoff); Windows IOCP backend present but README lists Windows as planned
integration.thread_safety: One Loop per thread; loop.stop() and submission must happen on the loop's own thread; cross-thread wakeups go through xev.Async and an optional shared thread pool

gotchas: Harness note (HttpArena libxev entry): the response carries only Content-Type, Content-Length and Connection headers, about 86 bytes per response against libreactorng's about 109 (bandwidth divided by rps, derived from page data), the handler does no routing (every path gets the sum) while libreactorng dispatches /pipeline, /baseline11, /baseline2 and 404s, and libxev is enrolled only in baseline, limited-conn and the three latency profiles, not pipelined; all three tilt slightly toward libxev, so the +0.1% baseline edge is not a win.

Harness note: HttpArena reports the best of N runs, and the top baseline-4096 entries cluster at 4.38-4.44 M req/s (libxev 4,381,919, libreactorng 4,377,377, zeemo 4,422,489, zix 4,442,329) at what scripts/lib/profiles.sh calls 'the ~4.4M baseline peak', with the server at about 6,145% of its 6,400% CPU; differences under 1-2% there do not rank implementations.

The HttpArena server uses the single-shot TCP.write and discards the byte count, so a short write would silently truncate a response (libxev's queueWrite handles partial writes); its integer parser ignores '-' and clamps negative sums to 0, unlike libreactorng's signed parse. HttpArena's request templates (get.raw, post_cl.raw, post_chunked.raw) only carry positive values, so the measured numbers are unaffected.

Loop.init caps ring entries at a u13 (8191; error.TooManyEntries above) and completions are caller-owned memory that must stay valid and unaliased until their callback runs; reusing a queued completion is the root of several open issues (#169, #227, #234).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick libxev when you want a reusable, cross-platform event-loop library for Zig or C; the HttpArena siblings (Rust raw tokio 4,187,085 req/s, tokio-uring 3,565,878, zix 4,442,329, zeemo 4,422,489 on baseline-4096) are application servers or runtimes in other ecosystems, and tokio/tokio-uring are the Rust equivalents if you are not on Zig.
verified_claims_summary: HttpArena (Threadripper PRO 3995WX, server on 32 cores/64 threads, gcannon over loopback, 4096 keep-alive connections, 5 s, best of N runs; libxev entry built with Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native, libreactorng with gcc -O3 -march=native): baseline-4096 4,381,919 req/s vs libreactorng 4,377,377 (a tie), h2o 3,641,609 (1.20x), nginx 3,284,513 (1.33x) and Drogon 2,022,710 (2.17x); limited-conn-4096 2,672,662 vs libreactorng 2,685,717 (-0.5%). At fixed offered rates libxev used 20.31 vs 21.04 us CPU per request at 1 M req/s, 21.49 vs 25.21 us at 10 k req/s and 15.45 vs 15.63 us at 500 k req/s on 8 CPUs against libreactorng (p99 1.12 ms vs 7.49 ms on the last), and Drogon used 32.13, 31.96 and 21.30 us (all ratios derived from page data; h2o and nginx are not enrolled in those profiles).
status_note: Actively maintained (3.6k stars, 591 commits, last commit 2026-05-06, used by Ghostty and zml) and MIT-licensed; stable on Linux and macOS per its README, with Windows and some cancel/reuse paths still carrying open bugs, and no benchmark claims from the project itself.
